high_school: Honestly, the biggest thing in high school is to keep your options open while you figure out if this career is really for you.

Start with your classes. Take the courses that lead toward your field, and push yourself a little with AP, honors, or dual-enrollment if you can handle it. Don't forget English and writing, though. Whatever career you end up in, people who can write and talk clearly get ahead. Keep your grades up too, because that's what gets you into good schools and helps with scholarships.

Outside of class, pick one or two things and stick with them instead of joining ten clubs. Colleges would rather see you be an officer or team lead in something you care about than a name on a list. If you can, start your own little project, whether that's a blog, a small business, or a volunteer effort. It gives you something real to talk about.

I'd also try to see the actual work as early as possible. Ask a family friend or a neighbor if you can shadow them for a day, or look for a summer program. A lot of students find out they love it, and some find out they don't, and both are useful to learn at 16 rather than 22.

Finally, talk to people. Your counselor and teachers know more than you think, and most professionals are happy to give a student twenty minutes. Start looking at colleges and majors in your junior year so nothing catches you off guard, and apply for scholarships early. There are always more deadlines than you expect.
The reason I say all this is that high school is the cheapest time to explore. A few good activities and some early exposure will save you a lot of time and money later.
college: College is where you go from being interested in a field to actually being good at it, and I think grades are only part of that.

Pick a major that supports where you want to end up, or a closely related one with a minor that fills in the gaps. Mix the theory classes with ones where you build something or work on a real project, and use your electives to pick up skills that employers like, such as data analysis, public speaking, or basic management. Keep your GPA solid, especially in your major, since some employers screen on it.

The other big piece is experience. Try to get at least two internships before you graduate, and start looking as early as sophomore year. They're competitive, so if you don't land one right away, don't panic. Research with a professor, a campus job in the field, or a serious personal project all count, and keep a portfolio of what you've done so you can show it in interviews.
Get the certifications that people in your field actually look for, and ask your professors what the industry expects, because they usually know.

Please don't skip the networking. Join a professional organization, go to the career fair even when it feels awkward, and get to know two or three professors well enough that they'll write you a strong recommendation. Message alumni and ask how they got started. Most of them say yes. And use the career center, because they'll review your resume and run mock interviews for free.

Start applying for jobs six to nine months before you graduate. If your field needs grad school or a licensing exam, plan for that early too. Overall, the students who do best are the ones who treat college as more than just classes.
entry_level: For your first job, I'd tell you not to get too hung up on the title or even a small difference in pay. What matters most is whether you'll learn and whether you have a good manager and team around you. A decent company with a great mentor beats a famous name where nobody has time for you.

In the first three months, just soak it up. Ask lots of questions, take notes, and figure out how the team really makes decisions and who people go to for what. Nobody expects you to know everything yet, but they do expect you to be reliable and to learn fast.

On the skills side, get the basics of your craft down so your work is accurate and people can depend on it. Work on how you communicate, too. Write clear emails, speak up in meetings, and practice presenting your work. It's also worth learning how the business actually runs, like who the customers are and how the company makes money, because that's what lets you see where you fit.

Ask for feedback regularly instead of waiting for your yearly review, and then show that you acted on it. Keep a running list of what you've accomplished, with numbers when you can, because you'll want it when promotion time comes around. Raise your hand for the stretch assignments and the projects that involve other teams. That's how people notice you.

Try to find a mentor a few levels above you who isn't your direct boss, and get to know people outside your own team. If your company has a training or tuition budget, use it. Then plan on staying one to three years so you can show real results before you move on.
That first job sets your habits and your reputation, and people who build trust early get the better projects and the faster promotions.
mid_career: This is the stage where I see people either stall out or take off, and the difference is usually how deliberate they are.

First, think about what you want to be known for. Some people become the deep expert in one area, and others become the person who connects several areas together. Either is fine, but pick one and steer your work toward it by going after the bigger and more visible projects in that space.

Second, start leading before somebody gives you the title. Mentor the newer people, run a project, and coordinate across teams. You'll learn how to delegate, how to give feedback that doesn't make people defensive, and how to handle conflict. If someone offers you a formal management role, treat it as a chance to find out whether you actually enjoy managing people, because plenty of great individual contributors don't.

Don't be afraid to make a move. Changing teams, companies, or even cities is often the quickest route to a bigger role. I'd check in with yourself once a year and compare your pay, scope, and title to what the market is offering. An advanced degree or an executive program can help, but only if it clearly opens the next door, so don't do it just to do it.

Work on being visible outside your own company, too. Speak at an event, write something, or get involved in a professional group. Try to build a relationship with a senior leader who will speak up for you when promotions are decided. That sponsor makes a bigger difference than most people realize.
And take care of yourself. This stage usually has the heaviest workload, and burning out won't help your career. Keep learning new tools and trends as well so your skills don't go stale.
management: The hardest part of moving into leadership is that the skills that got you promoted before are not the ones that will get you promoted now.

The biggest change is in how you think about your job. You're no longer judged on what you produce yourself. You're judged on what your team accomplishes, so you have to get comfortable getting work done through other people. You'll also spend more time on strategy, priorities, and trade-offs than on tasks.

The skills to work on are mostly about people. Learn how to coach, hire well, give honest feedback, and have the difficult conversations instead of avoiding them. You also need to get comfortable with budgets, planning, and measuring performance, and you need to be able to explain things to executives in a clear way, with a short summary, the business case, and a recommendation.

On education, a leadership program or an executive course can help. An MBA makes sense if most of the leaders in your field have one, but it isn't necessary everywhere, so ask around before you spend the money. Read, too. Management books and case studies are useful, and so is talking to peers who have the job you want.

Networking matters even more at this level. Get to know senior executives, and ask them directly what they'd need to see from you to promote you. Most people never ask. Find a sponsor who will put your name forward and a mentor who has already done the job.

To show you're ready, take responsibility for a budget, a bigger team, or a project that crosses several departments, and deliver clear results. Develop a successor, because you can't be promoted if no one can replace you. And tell your leadership that you want the role so you're on their radar when something opens up. If there's no path where you are, be prepared to go elsewhere.
People get trusted with larger teams when they've shown they can develop others, manage resources, and think strategically.
